name: Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II
summary: The F-35 is a stealth fighter, shaped and coated so it is very hard for radar to see. It can fight other aircraft, attack targets on the ground and gather information with its powerful sensors. It is now the main fighter jet of the Royal Australian Air Force.
funFacts: There are three versions: the F-35A takes off from normal runways, the F-35B can hover and land vertically, and the F-35C lands on aircraft carriers.
Each pilot's helmet costs about US$400,000 and lets them look through the floor of the aircraft using cameras mounted around the jet.
Australia ordered 72 F-35As, and all of them had been delivered by the end of 2024.
Although its official name is Lightning II, many pilots call it the Panther.
spotterTips: Look for a chunky single-engine jet with two angled tail fins, a diamond-shaped nose and no missiles hanging under the wings, because it carries weapons inside to stay stealthy. It is much louder than most other jets at airshows.

melbourne.where: Watch for F-35As at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027), where the RAAF has flown it in displays, and on flypasts for big events such as Anzac Day.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 2 Operational Conversion Unit and No. 3 and No. 77 Squadrons at RAAF Base Williamtown, and No. 75 Squadron at RAAF Base Tindal)

name: Boeing F/A-18F Super Hornet
summary: The Super Hornet is a big, powerful twin-engine fighter built to fly from aircraft carriers. The F model has two seats, one for the pilot and one for a weapons officer who runs the sensors. Australia bought 24 of them in 2007 to replace its old F-111 bombers.
funFacts: US Navy crews call it the Rhino, partly because of a bump on top of its nose that holds an antenna.
It can carry an extra fuel tank with a hose and act as a flying fuel station to refuel other jets.
Even though it is bigger than the original Hornet, it has 42 per cent fewer structural parts.
The RAAF's first Super Hornets arrived at RAAF Base Amberley in Queensland on 26 March 2010.
spotterTips: Look for a large twin-engine jet with two tail fins that lean outwards and rectangular engine intakes under the wings. The F model has a long two-seat bubble canopy.

melbourne.where: RAAF Super Hornets have flown thrilling handling displays at the Australian Grand Prix at Albert Park and appeared at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027), including air-to-air refuelling demonstrations.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 1 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

name: Boeing EA-18G Growler
summary: The Growler is a Super Hornet turned into a flying electronic jammer. Instead of a gun it carries special pods that detect enemy radars and fill them with electronic noise, so other aircraft can fly safely. Australia is the only country apart from the United States to fly it.
funFacts: It shares more than 90 per cent of its parts with the Super Hornet, but the cannon was removed to make room for electronics.
Its wingtip missile rails were swapped for pods that listen for enemy radar signals.
Two crew members do the job that needed four people in the older EA-6B Prowler.
The RAAF's first Growlers made their public debut at the 2017 Avalon Airshow.
spotterTips: It looks almost exactly like a two-seat Super Hornet, so look for the bulky pods on the wingtips and large jamming pods hanging under the wings and body.

melbourne.where: The RAAF's first two Growlers flew in for their public debut at the 2017 Avalon Airshow near Geelong. Look for them at future Avalon Airshows (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 6 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

name: Boeing C-17 Globemaster III
summary: The C-17 is a giant military cargo plane that can carry tanks, helicopters and huge loads across the world, then land on short or rough runways. The RAAF uses its C-17s for everything from moving troops to delivering help after floods and bushfires.
funFacts: Crews nicknamed it The Moose because of the honking noise its fuel tank vents make during refuelling.
It can carry a 69-tonne M1 Abrams tank inside its cargo hold.
C-17s fly to Antarctica each summer, taking about five hours each way between New Zealand and McMurdo Station.
In August 2021 one C-17 carried 823 people out of Kabul in a single flight, a record for the type.
spotterTips: Look for a huge grey four-engine jet with wings mounted on top of the body, drooping wingtips with small winglets, and a tall T-shaped tail.

melbourne.where: RAAF C-17s have done low flypasts at the Australian Grand Prix at Albert Park and have flown over Melbourne, Port Phillip Bay and Geelong ahead of the Avalon Airshow (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 36 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

name: Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules
summary: The Super Hercules is the modern version of the famous Hercules, a tough four-propeller transport that can land on short dirt strips. It carries troops, vehicles and supplies, and drops paratroopers and aid by parachute. Australia flies the stretched C-130J-30 model.
funFacts: Each propeller has six curved blades, compared with four on older Hercules.
The more powerful engines and propellers changed how the wing stalled, so engineers added a stick pusher system and testing was delayed by nine months.
The stretched C-130J-30 is 4.6 metres longer and can carry 92 paratroopers.
Australia ordered 20 more C-130J-30s in July 2023.
spotterTips: Look for a high-wing transport with four propeller engines, each with six scimitar-shaped blades, and an upswept tail with a loading ramp underneath.

melbourne.where: RAAF C-130Js have flown over Melbourne, Port Phillip Bay and Geelong to promote the Avalon Airshow, and often appear at the show itself (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 37 Squadron, RAAF Base Richmond, New South Wales)

name: Airbus KC-30A (A330 MRTT)
summary: The KC-30A is an Airbus A330 airliner turned into a flying petrol station. It can pass fuel to fighter jets and other aircraft in mid-air, so they can fly much further. It can also carry passengers and cargo at the same time.
funFacts: The RAAF received the first A330 tanker delivered to any customer, handed over at RAAF Base Amberley on 1 June 2011.
It can refuel aircraft two ways: with a long boom under the tail, or with hoses that trail from pods under each wing.
The refuelling operator sits in the cockpit and watches the refuelling on 2D and 3D screens.
One RAAF KC-30A has a VIP fit-out and has flown the Prime Minister overseas.
spotterTips: It looks like an A330 airliner in military grey, but look for the refuelling boom under the tail and the hose pods hanging under each wing.

melbourne.where: KC-30As have performed air-to-air refuelling demonstrations with fighter jets at the Avalon Airshow (next held in 2027) and took part in the 2014 Centenary of Military Aviation air show at RAAF Williams, Point Cook.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 33 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

name: Boeing P-8A Poseidon
summary: The P-8A Poseidon is a Boeing 737 airliner rebuilt to hunt submarines and keep watch over the ocean. It searches huge areas of sea for ships and submarines, and also helps with search and rescue. Australia guards a very long coastline, so these aircraft are very important to the RAAF.
funFacts: It is based on the Boeing 737-800, the same type of airliner many people fly on holidays.
It drops sonobuoys, small floating listening devices that hear submarines underwater and radio the sounds back to the aircraft.
It works together with the MQ-4C Triton, a large robot aircraft that flies very long surveillance missions.
The RAAF has 14 P-8As, with the last one delivered in May 2026.
spotterTips: It looks like a grey Boeing 737, but has no passenger windows along most of the body, raked wingtips with no winglets, and lots of antennas on the belly.

melbourne.where: A P-8A from No. 11 Squadron flew at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong in 2025. Look for it again at the next show in 2027.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 11, No. 12 and No. 292 Squadrons, RAAF Base Edinburgh, South Australia)

name: Boeing E-7A Wedgetail
role: Airborne early warning and control aircraft
summary: The Wedgetail is a flying radar station built from a Boeing 737. Its big radar can watch the sky and sea for hundreds of kilometres in every direction, and its crew directs friendly aircraft like air traffic controllers in the sky. It was developed for Australia first, and now other air forces are buying it too.
funFacts: It is named after the wedge-tailed eagle, Australia's largest bird of prey.
The radar does not spin like older radar dishes. It steers its beam electronically instead.
The flat radar on its back is nicknamed the top hat.
Australia has six, all flown by No. 2 Squadron.
spotterTips: Look for a grey Boeing 737 with a long, flat, blade-like radar mounted on top of the body, plus small fins under the tail.

melbourne.where: An E-7A was on static display at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong in 2025, where visitors could see it up close. Look for it again at the next show in 2027.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 2 Squadron, RAAF Base Williamtown, New South Wales)

name: Pilatus PC-21
summary: The PC-21 is the aircraft every new RAAF pilot learns to fly on. It has a propeller, but it is so fast and agile, with a cockpit like a modern fighter, that students can learn many jet skills in it. It is also flown by the Roulettes, the RAAF's aerobatic display team.
funFacts: Pilatus says it can match speeds and climb rates that used to need a jet trainer.
Australia ordered 49 PC-21s in 2015, and all were delivered by November 2019.
The Roulettes fly seven PC-21s, including one spare.
Its cockpit screens can pretend to show radar and weapons, so students practise fighter skills without real ones.
spotterTips: Look for a sleek single-propeller aircraft with a five-bladed propeller, a long bubble canopy with two seats one behind the other, and a fighter-like shape. The Roulettes' aircraft are painted red, white and blue.

melbourne.where: Your best chance in Victoria. PC-21s are based at RAAF Base East Sale in Gippsland, home of the Roulettes and pilot training. The Roulettes perform at the Australian Grand Prix at Albert Park and at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (Central Flying School and the Roulettes at RAAF Base East Sale, Victoria, and No. 2 Flying Training School at RAAF Base Pearce, Western Australia)

name: BAE Systems Hawk 127
specsVariant: Hawk 128 (RAAF Hawk 127s have been upgraded to a similar standard)
engines: 1 × Rolls-Royce Turbomeca Adour turbofan (Mk 871 on the RAAF Hawk 127)
summary: The Hawk is a small, nimble jet trainer. After learning on the PC-21, RAAF pilots move to the Hawk to get ready for fast jets like the F-35A. It is one of the most successful jet trainers ever made.
funFacts: The famous Red Arrows display team in the United Kingdom flies Hawks.
Australia ordered 33 Hawk 127s in 1997. Twelve were built in the UK and 21 were built in Australia.
The Hawk first flew in 1974, more than 50 years ago, and is still in service.
Australian Hawks were upgraded so their cockpits work like those of modern fighters.
spotterTips: Look for a small two-seat jet with a long stepped canopy, low wings, and engine intakes on each side of the body just behind the cockpit.

melbourne.where: RAAF Hawks have appeared at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027). They are based interstate, so sightings in Victoria are less common.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 76 Squadron at RAAF Base Williamtown, New South Wales, and No. 79 Squadron at RAAF Base Pearce, Western Australia)

name: Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor
summary: The F-22 Raptor was the world's first stealth fighter built mainly to win battles in the air against other fighters. It combines stealth, speed and amazing agility. Only the United States Air Force flies it, because the US never allowed it to be sold overseas.
funFacts: It can supercruise, flying faster than sound at about 1,870 km/h without using its afterburners.
Its engine nozzles move up and down to push the jet around, so it can do tight, slow manoeuvres that look impossible.
Production stopped in 2011 after only 195 were built.
Australia's Chief of the Defence Force said in 2008 that Australia was interested in buying the F-22.
spotterTips: Look for a large twin-engine stealth jet with angled edges, two outward-leaning tail fins, diamond-shaped wings and flat, square engine nozzles at the back.

melbourne.where: US Air Force F-22s have flown spectacular displays at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong several times, including 2013, 2017, 2023 and 2025. The next show is in 2027.

name: Northrop B-2 Spirit
summary: The B-2 Spirit is a stealth bomber shaped like a giant boomerang. It is a flying wing with no tail at all, designed to be almost invisible to radar. Only 21 were ever built, making it one of the rarest and most expensive aircraft in the world.
funFacts: The 21 aircraft cost a total of US$44.7 billion, about US$2.13 billion each.
It has no tail fins. Computers keep it stable by moving control surfaces on the back edge of the wing.
Its wingspan of 52.4 metres is more than twice as long as its body.
All B-2s are based at Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri and live in climate-controlled hangars to protect their special coatings.
spotterTips: You cannot mistake it: a huge dark grey flying wing with no tail and a saw-tooth (zigzag) back edge.

name: Boeing B-52 Stratofortress
crew: 5 (pilot, co-pilot, weapon systems officer, navigator and electronic warfare officer)
summary: The B-52 is a gigantic eight-engine bomber that first flew in 1952. The US Air Force has kept upgrading it for more than 70 years, and it can carry a huge load over very long distances. It is planned to keep flying until about 2050.
funFacts: If it serves until 2050 as planned, it will have been in service for about 95 years, longer than any other military aircraft type.
It has eight jet engines, hung in pairs under its long drooping wings.
The last B-52H was delivered in 1962, and those same aircraft are still flying today.
The engines are planned to be replaced, turning the B-52H into the B-52J.
spotterTips: Look for a very long, slender bomber with eight engines in four pairs under thin drooping wings, a tall tail fin, and small wheels near the wingtips.

melbourne.where: US Air Force B-52s have visited the Avalon Airshow near Geelong several times, including a static display in 2015, a visit in 2019 and a flyover in 2023. The next show is in 2027, but visits depend on US operations.

name: Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II
summary: The A-10 was built to fly low and slow to protect soldiers on the ground. It is extremely tough and was designed around an enormous cannon in its nose. It is not pretty, which is why everyone calls it the Warthog.
funFacts: The whole aircraft was designed around its huge 30 mm GAU-8 Avenger rotary cannon.
The pilot sits in a tub of titanium armour weighing about 540 kg, nicknamed the bathtub.
It is named after the P-47 Thunderbolt, a famous fighter from the Second World War.
Its retirement has been planned many times, but in April 2026 the US Air Force delayed it until 2030.
spotterTips: Look for straight, thick wings, two big round engines mounted high on the back of the body, and twin tail fins at the very end.

name: General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon
summary: The F-16 is a small, light and very agile fighter, and one of the most successful jets ever made. More than 4,600 have been built and it is flown by air forces all over the world. Pilots and crews call it the Viper.
funFacts: Its first flight on 20 January 1974 was an accident. During a fast taxi test it started to wobble, so the pilot took off rather than risk crashing.
It was one of the first fighters with fly-by-wire controls, where computers help fly the plane.
The pilot's seat is tilted back 30 degrees to help cope with strong g-forces.
Its frameless bubble canopy gives the pilot a superb view in every direction.
spotterTips: Look for a small single-engine jet with one tail fin, a big air intake under the cockpit (like an open mouth) and a clear bubble canopy.

melbourne.where: F-16s have performed at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong. The Republic of Singapore Air Force Black Knights flew F-16s in 2015, and a US Air Force F-16 took part in 2025. The next show is in 2027.
melbourne.operators: Republic of Singapore Air Force and United States Air Force (visiting)

name: Eurofighter Typhoon
manufacturer: Eurofighter GmbH (Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo)
country: United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Spain
summary: The Typhoon is a fast and agile fighter built by a team of four European countries working together. It was designed first to win fights against other aircraft, and later gained the ability to attack ground targets too. It is flown by several air forces in Europe and the Middle East.
funFacts: It was built jointly by the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Spain, with parts made in different countries.
It is deliberately unstable, so computers make thousands of tiny corrections to keep it flying smoothly.
It can reach about Mach 2.35, more than twice the speed of sound.
Its small front wings, called canards, help make it very agile.
spotterTips: Look for a triangle-shaped (delta) wing, small canard wings just behind the cockpit, a single tail fin and a large air intake under the nose.

name: Dassault Rafale
summary: The Rafale is France's main fighter, able to do almost every combat job, from air defence to reconnaissance. One version can fly from France's aircraft carrier. It has become popular overseas, with hundreds more on order.
funFacts: Rafale is French for gust of wind.
The first demonstrator, the Rafale A, flew in 1986, and the production Rafale C followed in 1991.
The navy version flies from the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle.
Tests showed it could land on a carrier while still carrying heavy loads of unused weapons.
spotterTips: Look for a delta wing with small canards near the cockpit, two engines side by side, a single tail fin and curved air intakes under the wing roots.

name: Saab JAS 39 Gripen
summary: The Gripen is a small, clever Swedish fighter designed to be cheap to run and easy to look after. Sweden wanted it to be able to hide away from big airbases and operate from ordinary roads. It is flown by several countries, including Sweden, Hungary, Brazil and Thailand.
funFacts: It was designed to take off and land on stretches of public road that Sweden set up as emergency runways.
A small ground crew can refuel and rearm it quickly, even at a road base.
JAS stands for the Swedish words for fighter, attack and reconnaissance, because one aircraft does all three jobs.
A newer, bigger version called the Gripen E has a more powerful General Electric engine.
spotterTips: Look for a small single-engine jet with a delta wing, canards just behind the cockpit, and curved air intakes on each side of the body.

name: Sukhoi Su-57
summary: The Su-57 is Russia's first stealth fighter. It is large, fast and very manoeuvrable, but only a small number have been built so far. It entered service with the Russian Aerospace Forces in 2020.
funFacts: NATO countries give Russian aircraft code names, and the Su-57's is Felon.
It came from a program called PAK FA, which started in 1999.
It can supercruise at about 1,400 km/h without using afterburners.
Its engine nozzles can swivel to help it perform very tight manoeuvres.
spotterTips: Look for a long, flat stealth fighter with widely spaced engines, all-moving twin tail fins and small moving panels at the front of each wing root.

name: Lockheed C-5 Galaxy
summary: The C-5 Galaxy is the biggest aircraft in the US Air Force and one of the largest military aircraft in the world. Its whole nose lifts up and its tail opens, so huge loads can drive straight through. All the remaining aircraft have been upgraded to the C-5M Super Galaxy.
funFacts: Its nose swings upwards like a giant visor so vehicles can drive in at the front.
It can kneel, lowering itself so the cargo floor is at the height of a truck tray for easy loading.
It can carry 36 cargo pallets, about 127 tonnes of cargo.
It is the largest aircraft able to fly to Antarctica, landing near McMurdo Station.
spotterTips: Look for a gigantic grey four-engine jet with wings mounted high on the body, drooping wings and a tall T-shaped tail. It is noticeably bigger than a C-17.

melbourne.where: A US Air Force C-5 Galaxy was on display at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong in 2023, and visitors could look inside. The next show is in 2027, but visiting aircraft change each time.

name: Airbus A400M Atlas
crew: 3 or 4 (2 pilots, optional third pilot and 1 loadmaster)
summary: The A400M is a big European transport aircraft that sits between the C-130 Hercules and the C-17 in size. It can carry heavy vehicles and helicopters, drop paratroopers, and even refuel other aircraft in flight. It is flown by several European air forces.
funFacts: The two propellers on each wing spin in opposite directions, which is very unusual.
Its TP400 engines are among the most powerful turboprops ever built in the West.
Before its first flight, the engine was tested by bolting it onto a C-130 Hercules.
It can carry 116 fully equipped troops or up to 37 tonnes of cargo.
spotterTips: Look for a high-wing transport with four large propellers with curved, scimitar-shaped blades, a T-tail and a big rear loading ramp.

melbourne.where: A French Air Force A400M was on static display at the 2015 Avalon Airshow near Geelong, and a German A400M visited in 2025. The next show is in 2027.
melbourne.operators: French Air and Space Force and German Air Force (visiting)

name: Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey
engines: 2 × Rolls-Royce T406-AD-400 turboshafts driving tilting rotors
crew: 3 to 4 (pilot, co-pilot and 1 or 2 crew chiefs or loadmasters)
summary: The Osprey is a tiltrotor: it takes off like a helicopter, then tilts its giant rotors forward to fly like an aeroplane. This means it can land almost anywhere but travel much faster and further than a helicopter. It is mainly flown by the US Marine Corps.
funFacts: Each rotor is about 11.6 metres across, so it cannot land like a normal aeroplane with the rotors pointed forward.
For storage on ships, the wing swivels and the rotors fold so it takes up much less space.
It can carry 24 seated troops or a small vehicle inside.
US Marine Corps Ospreys spend several months a year in northern Australia as part of the Marine Rotational Force in Darwin.
spotterTips: Look for a chunky grey aircraft with a big rotor on each wingtip that can point up like a helicopter or forward like propellers, plus twin tail fins.

melbourne.where: Not often seen in Victoria. US Marine Corps MV-22B Ospreys deploy to RAAF Base Darwin each year with the Marine Rotational Force and train around northern Australia, including Townsville.

name: McDonnell Douglas AV-8B Harrier II
manufacturer: McDonnell Douglas and British Aerospace (now Boeing and BAE Systems)
role: Vertical or short take-off ground attack aircraft
summary: The Harrier II is a jump jet that can take off and land vertically, and even hover in mid-air like a helicopter. This lets it fly from small ships and rough clearings without a long runway. The US Marine Corps retired its Harriers in June 2026, but Spain and Italy still fly them from their ships.
funFacts: Its single engine has four swivelling nozzles that point down to hover and backwards to fly fast.
A heavily loaded Harrier usually uses a short rolling take-off, because it can lift more that way than straight up.
It mostly flies from small aircraft carriers and amphibious assault ships.
It is being replaced by the F-35B, which can also hover and land vertically.
spotterTips: Look for a small jet with wings that droop downwards, big round intakes on each side of the cockpit, and nozzles on the sides of the body instead of at the back.

name: Grumman F-14 Tomcat
summary: The F-14 Tomcat was a big, fast US Navy fighter famous for its swing wings and its starring role in the film Top Gun. It protected aircraft carriers from attack for more than 30 years. The US Navy retired it in 2006, and today only Iran still operates a few.
funFacts: Its wings swing forward for slow flying and landing, and sweep back for high-speed flight.
The US Navy retired its last Tomcats on 22 September 2006.
It became famous after the 1986 film Top Gun, and some Navy pilots who flew it worked on the movie.
After it retired, the US stopped selling spare parts so they could not reach Iran's Tomcats.
spotterTips: Look for a large twin-tail fighter with wings that can sweep back, two widely spaced engines and a long two-seat canopy. You will most likely see one in a museum.

name: Lockheed U-2
summary: The U-2 is a spy plane that flies so high, more than 21 kilometres up, that pilots must wear spacesuit-like pressure suits. It has huge glider-like wings and takes photos and gathers information from far above everyone else. It first flew in 1955 and the US Air Force is now slowly retiring it.
funFacts: It is so hard to land that a second U-2 pilot chases it down the runway in a fast car, calling out its height by radio.
It has wheels only under the body, so small wheels called pogos hold the wings up for take-off and simply fall off.
Its wingtips have titanium skids for when a wing touches down at the end of a landing.
It outlasted the SR-71 Blackbird, the faster jet that was meant to replace it.
spotterTips: Look for a dark grey jet with extremely long, thin, straight wings like a glider, a slim body and a single tail fin.
